about: Today’s street centrelines of each town, each segment dated by the oldest georeferenced sheet over the town that draws it (the Government Survey’s maps of the islands from 1881 to 1903, the U.S. Geological Survey’s quadrangles from 1910 to 1963 and of about 2000), found on each sheet by its line, and borne out by the later sheets. Every date is a date by which the street was there.
rule: Each segment is cut into pieces of about 80 m, sampled every 2.5 m along it, 7 m short of its ends. A sheet pixel is ink where it is darker than 0.65 of the sheet's paper (the 80th percentile of brightness over the export tile), or the share the sheet's own `ink` gives. A piece is found on a sheet where, at some offset within 15 m of it, at least 62% of its samples are ink or within a pixel of ink, and at some offset within 10 m, at least 60% are paper. Each sheet is first moved over the town by the shift that finds the most pieces (searched within 300 m for the Government Survey's island maps, 80 m for the quadrangles, by 20 m, then by 5 m and by a pixel), then over each 1200 m cell holding at least 40 pieces by its own shift within 75 or 20 m of that; each move costs as many pieces as 5% of those searched at the edge of its search, less nearer in, so a sheet stays where the State placed it unless the streets say otherwise. A piece is found on one of the Government Survey's island maps only where at least 75% of its samples are ink, without the pixel's grace, and 65% paper; it is dated by the oldest sheet that finds it, if at least half the later sheets that cover it find it too and, for an island map, another island map finds it too where two or more cover it; a segment by the year by which half its dated length is dated, where at least 30% of its length is dated at all; any other segment by the centreline layer’s own year.
